_note: Copy is deliberately short. The page exists to get people to the map and the videos, not to read an essay. Claim = one sentence. Essay = two short paragraphs, folded away. Every video is a site walkthrough wired to a known site, so each carries its own 'sites' list and draws its own mini-map.

machining.name: Machining
machining.headline: Tool marks that repeat on four continents.
machining.claim: Striations, bore holes, saw kerfs and flat-planed faces that look mechanical. Four continents, no contact between them, and stone their documented toolkits were not supposed to cut.
essay: Each of these has a local explanation, and the local explanations don't resemble each other. Bazda's grooves are Roman quarrying. Longyou's are a lost Chinese chisel technique. The Serapeum's boxes are Ptolemaic bull burials. Every one is plausible on its own ground. None explains why the marks look alike.

Two caveats. Similar marks can come from different processes; appearance is not method. And a photograph flattens the evidence that would settle it: depth, pitch, tolerance, tool-nose radius. These are the best substitute for standing there with a straightedge. They are not measurement.
machining.videos_note: Comparative studies rather than site walkthroughs, which is why they never fitted on a site page.

precision.name: Precision
precision.headline: Tolerances you would ask a machine shop for.
precision.claim: Joints you cannot slide paper into. Surfaces flat to a fraction of a millimetre, corners cut square in granite, and the tolerance holds across whole buildings rather than one showpiece block.
essay: Precision is measurable, which makes it the most testable thing in the Atlas. A flat face is either flat or it isn't. A joint either takes a feeler gauge or it doesn't. That is why it belongs in a comparative view: the question is not whether one wall is impressive, it is whether the same tolerance turns up in places with no contact.
What a video cannot give you is the number. Treat these as a survey of where to look, not as evidence of a figure.
precision.videos_note: Walkthroughs where the camera actually gets close enough to see the joint.

polygonal.name: Polygonal
polygonal.headline: No two blocks alike, and no mortar anywhere.
polygonal.claim: Many-sided stones cut to fit each other rather than to a standard. No vertical joint runs the height of the wall, so when the ground moves the wall flexes instead of failing.
essay: Square your stone and you can stack fast, but the courses run straight through and that is exactly where a wall fails when the ground moves. Fit each block to its neighbours and the empty joints act as energy sinks. That is the practical reason the technique recurs on five continents.
What it doesn't explain is the tolerance at the top of the range, or joint faces that curve in two directions so a block cannot be lowered straight in along any axis.
polygonal.videos_note: Six walls, six countries, no contact between any of them.

geometry.name: Geometry
geometry.headline: The same shapes, drawn by people who never met.
geometry.claim: Circles, spirals, cup-and-ring marks, precise alignments and repeated proportions. Every inhabited continent carries some of them, in cultures with no route between them.
essay: Geometry is the easiest pattern to over-read, because humans find shapes everywhere and a circle is not a fingerprint. The useful version of the question is narrower: not "do circles recur", but do specific constructions recur: the same alignment, the same ratio, the same motif executed the same way.
So these are chosen for what is on the stone rather than what is claimed about it.
geometry.videos_note: Marks and layouts, filmed close. Read the shapes before reading anyone's theory of them.

scale.name: Scale
scale.headline: Stones no recorded method could move.
scale.claim: Blocks from 50 to 1,500 tons, quarried, dressed, and in most cases carried somewhere else, by people whose documented toolkit was rope, timber and muscle.
essay: Scale is the pattern people meet first and understand least, because a photograph cannot transmit mass. Numbers do not fix that either: 1,764,000 lb means nothing to a body. The translation that lands is people: 2,205 of them pushing at the same instant, just to start the Trilithon sliding.
You can stand next to six of these stones in Feel the Weight, at 1.7 m eye height, with a truck and a double-decker parked alongside for calibration.
scale.videos_note: The heaviest worked stones on earth, filmed from the ground. Then go and stand next to them.

hardness.name: Hardness
hardness.headline: Stone harder than the tools that shaped it.
hardness.claim: Granite, diorite, basalt and andesite, 6 to 7 on Mohs, worked to a finish by cultures whose surviving tools are copper and stone. Softer does not cut harder.
essay: This is the criterion where the arithmetic is hardest to wave away. Copper is about 3 on Mohs; granite is 6 to 7. Softer does not cut harder. The orthodox answer is abrasion, meaning sand, dolerite pounders and time, and for rough shaping it plainly works. The argument is about the finish, and about how long the numbers say it should have taken.
Only 31 sites in the Atlas carry this tag, which is under-tagging rather than scarcity. Treat the count as a floor.
hardness.videos_note: Includes one experiment: someone actually trying to carve basalt the orthodox way.

stratigraphy.name: Stratigraphy
stratigraphy.headline: Ground that argues with the date on the sign.
stratigraphy.claim: Weathering, sediment and buried courses that read older than the date on the sign. The one criterion where the evidence sits under the building rather than in it.
essay: This is the most contested thing the Atlas tracks, and the tag means a dispute exists, not that it has been settled. Geological dating of a monument is genuinely hard: erosion rates vary, fill gets redeposited, and a buried course can mean an older phase or a later repair.
So these are collected as the argument rather than the answer. Where a claim is disputed in the literature, that dispute is the point of the page.
stratigraphy.videos_note: Contested dating, filmed at the section rather than argued from a chair.
